# CLOOB: MODERN HOPFIELD NETWORKS WITH INFOLOOB OUTPERFORM CLIP

Anonymous authors

Paper under double-blind review

# ABSTRACT

Contrastive learning with the InfoNCE objective is exceptionally successful in various self-supervised learning tasks. Recently, the CLIP model yielded impressive results on zero-shot transfer learning when using InfoNCE for learning visual representations from natural language supervision. However, InfoNCE as a lower bound on the mutual information has been shown to perform poorly for high mutual information. In contrast, the InfoLOOB upper bound (leave one out bound) works well for high mutual information but suffers from large variance and instabilities. We introduce "Contrastive Leave One Out Boost" (CLOOB), where modern Hopfield networks boost learning with the InfoLOOB objective. Modern Hopfield networks replace the original embeddings by retrieved embeddings in the InfoLOOB objective. The retrieved embeddings give InfoLOOB two assets. Firstly, the retrieved embeddings stabilize InfoLOOB, since they are less noisy and more similar to one another than the original embeddings. Secondly, they are enriched by correlations, since the covariance structure of embeddings is reinforced through retrievals. We compare CLOOB to CLIP after learning on the Conceptual Captions and the YFCC dataset with respect to their zero-shot transfer learning performance on other datasets. CLOOB consistently outperforms CLIP at zero-shot transfer learning across all considered architectures and datasets.

# 1 INTRODUCTION

With the advent of large corpora of unlabeled data in vision and language, self-supervised learning has become highly successful. Most of the self-supervised learning techniques are based on contrastive learning, for which either views of images are contrasted with views of other images or text descriptions of images are contrasted with text descriptions of other images. Some contrastive learning objectives, such as those of BYOL (Grill et al., 2020) and SimSiam (Chen & He, 2021), do not require negative samples. However, the most popular objective for contrastive learning is InfoNCE (van den Oord et al., 2018), in which for an anchor sample, a positive sample is contrasted with negative samples.

The idea to use objectives with negative samples is well known in deep learning (Chen et al., 2017; Mikolov et al., 2013). Also noise-contrastive estimation (NCE) uses negative (random noise) samples to contrast them with the data, in order to estimate normalizing constants for statistical models (Gutmann & Hyvärinen, 2010). InfoNCE has been derived from NCE, while it has been introduced as Contrastive Predictive Coding (CPC) (van den Oord et al., 2018) to learn abstract representations in an unsupervised way. Via CPC, InfoNCE has already been used for transfer learning (Hénaff et al., 2019). InfoNCE has been applied to natural language response suggestion (Henderson et al., 2017), to learning sentence representations from unlabelled data (Logeswaran & Lee, 2018) and to unsupervised feature learning by maximizing distinctions between instances (Wu et al., 2018). Pretext-Invariant Representation Learning (PIRL) also uses InfoNCE to contrast representations of transformed versions of the same image with representations of other images (Misra & vanDerMaaten, 2020). Also Momentum Contrast (MoCo) for unsupervised visual representation learning is based on InfoNCE (He et al., 2020). MoCo uses a dynamic dictionary with a queue and a moving-averaged encoder to build large dictionaries for negative examples. SimCLR is a well known approach that is based on InfoNCE for contrastive learning of visual representations, which was highly effective for transfer learning (Chen et al., 2020). Good performance at zero-shot transfer learning (Lampert et al., 2009) is one of the most ambitious goals in vision, since it would improve various real

world downstream applications. Current models in natural language processing and vision often underperform at real-world applications. While they perform very well on standard benchmarks, they fail at new data, new applications, deployments in the wild, and stress tests (D'Amour et al., 2020; Recht et al., 2019a; Taori et al., 2020). Therefore, practitioners doubt these models and hesitate to employ them in real world application. A model with high zero-shot transfer learning performance is supposed to perform well when deployed in real world applications, therefore will be trusted by practitioners.

Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP) yielded very impressive results at zero-shot transfer learning (Radford et al., 2021a;b) and is the largest success story of InfoNCE so far. CLIP learns expressive image embeddings directly from raw text, thereby leveraging a much richer source of supervision than just labels. The CLIP model has the potential to become one of the most important foundation models (Bommasani et al., 2021). Since the introduction of the CLIP model, there were a plethora of follow-up publications (see Appendix Section A.5). Though CLIP is a big success at zero-shot transfer learning, it can be improved. The training of a CLIP model saturates in early learning phases, since it suffers from an "explaining away" problem (Wellman & Henrion, 1993). Training hardly increases the similarity between a text and a corresponding image, if the text can identify the image in a mini-batch of images and vice versa. This saturation effect even appears, when the similarity can be easily increased. The saturation stems from InfoNCE objective, which has the form  $a / (a + b)$  with  $a$  giving the similarity of a matched pair and  $b$  giving the sum of similarities of unmatched pairs. For a large similarity  $a$ , the objective saturates and increasing  $a$  has a small effect. In contrast, we will use an objective of the form  $a / b$  which does not saturate. However, such an objective is not stable and has high variance for small  $b$ . Besides the "explaining away" effect, CLIP suffers from extracting correlations in the original data. These correlations can stem from co-occurrences of related words in text or from co-occurrences of objects, textures, or colors in images. We introduce "Contrastive Leave One Out Boost" (CLOOB) which overcomes the problems of CLIP namely (i) "explaining away" that leads to saturation and (ii) missing correlations in the data. CLOOB uses the leave-one-out ("InfoLOOB") objective (Poole et al., 2019) in combination with modern Hopfield networks (Ramsauer et al., 2021; 2020; Widrich et al., 2020). Modern Hopfield networks stabilize the InfoLOOB objective and reinforce correlations in the data. In CLOOB, modern Hopfield networks replace the original embeddings by retrieved embeddings. The retrieved embeddings come with two advantages. Firstly, the retrieved embeddings are less noisy and more similar to one another than the original embeddings. This stabilizes the InfoLOOB loss function as  $b$  is larger. Secondly, the retrieved embeddings have an enriched correlation structure through co-occurrences of embedding features. The retrieved embedding is an average over stored embeddings that are similar to the original embedding, therefore co-occurrences are reinforced.

# Our contributions are

(a) we introduce a new contrastive learning method called CLOOB,  
(b) we propose InfoLOOB as an objective for contrastive learning,  
(c) we propose to use modern Hopfield networks to increase stability and to reinforce correlations for contrastive learning,  
(d) we show theoretical properties of the InfoLOOB objective and loss function.

# 2 INFOLOOB VS. INFONCE

We derive bounds on the mutual information between random variables  $X$  and  $Y$  distributed according to  $p(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y})$ . The mutual information  $\mathrm{I}(X;Y)$  between random variables  $X$  and  $Y$  is

$$
\operatorname {I} (X; Y) = \operatorname {E} _ {p (\boldsymbol {x}, \boldsymbol {y})} \left[ \ln \frac {p (\boldsymbol {x} , \boldsymbol {y})}{p (\boldsymbol {x}) p (\boldsymbol {y})} \right] = \operatorname {E} _ {p (\boldsymbol {x}, \boldsymbol {y})} \left[ \ln \frac {p (\boldsymbol {x} \mid \boldsymbol {y})}{p (\boldsymbol {x})} \right] = \operatorname {E} _ {p (\boldsymbol {x}, \boldsymbol {y})} \left[ \ln \frac {p (\boldsymbol {y} \mid \boldsymbol {x})}{p (\boldsymbol {y})} \right]. (1)
$$

The multi-sample lower bound "InfoNCE" has been introduced in van den Oord et al. (2018). Here a pair of an anchor sample  $\pmb{y}$  and a positive sample  $\pmb{x}_1$  is drawn according to the joint distribution  $p(\pmb{x}_1, \pmb{y})$ . The negative samples  $\tilde{X} = \{\pmb{x}_2, \dots, \pmb{x}_N\}$  are drawn iid according to the marginal distribution  $p(\pmb{x})$  giving the set  $X = \{\pmb{x}_1, \pmb{x}_2, \dots, \pmb{x}_N\}$  of one positive and  $N - 1$  negative samples. The datasets probabilities are  $p(\tilde{X}) = \prod_{i=2}^{N} p(\pmb{x}_i)$ ,  $p(X \mid \pmb{y}) = p(\pmb{x}_1 \mid \pmb{y}) \prod_{i=2}^{N} p(\pmb{x}_i)$ , and

$p(X) = \prod_{i=1}^{N} p(\boldsymbol{x}_i)$ . The InfoNCE with score function  $f(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{y})$  is defined as

$$
\operatorname {I} _ {\text {I n f o N C E}} \left(X _ {1}; Y\right) = \operatorname {E} _ {p (\boldsymbol {y})} \left[ \operatorname {E} _ {p (X | \boldsymbol {y})} \left[ \ln \left(\frac {f \left(\boldsymbol {x} _ {1} , \boldsymbol {y}\right)}{\frac {1}{N} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {N} f \left(\boldsymbol {x} _ {i} , \boldsymbol {y}\right)}\right) \right] \right], \tag {2}
$$

where the factor  $1 / N$  leads to the additive constant  $\ln N$ , where we follow Poole et al. (2019); Tschannen et al. (2019); Cheng et al. (2020); Chen et al. (2021). For  $f(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{y}) = p(\boldsymbol{y} \mid \boldsymbol{x})$  we obtain the InfoNCE with probabilities. The InfoNCE is a lower bound on the mutual information, which is stated in the next theorem.

Theorem 1 (InfoNCE lower bound). InfoNCE with score function  $f(\pmb{x}, \pmb{y})$  is a lower bound on the mutual information:

$$
\operatorname {I} \left(X _ {1}; Y\right) \geq \operatorname {E} _ {p (\boldsymbol {y})} \left[ \operatorname {E} _ {p (X | \boldsymbol {y})} \left[ \ln \left(\frac {f (\boldsymbol {x} _ {1} , \boldsymbol {y})}{\frac {1}{N} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {N} f (\boldsymbol {x} _ {i} , \boldsymbol {y})}\right) \right] \right] = \operatorname {I} _ {\text {I n f o N C E}} \left(X _ {1}; Y\right). \tag {3}
$$

In particular, the bound holds for InfoNCE with probabilities, i.e. for  $f(\pmb{x}, \pmb{y}) = p(\pmb{y} \mid \pmb{x})$ .

For a proof see Poole et al. (2019) and the proof of Theorem A1 in the Appendix.

In Poole et al. (2019), a variational upper bound on the mutual information called "Leave one out upper bound" was introduced. In Cheng et al. (2020) this bound is called "L1Out". For simplicity, we call this bound "InfoLOOB", where LOOB is an acronym for "Leave One Out Bound". InfoLOOB is similar to InfoNCE except that the denominator (Eq. (3)) does not contain the positive sample  $x_{1}$ . We want to use InfoLOOB as an objective, since it approximates the mutual information better than InfoNCE, in particular for large mutual information values (see next section).

The InfoLOOB with score function  $f(\pmb{x}, \pmb{y})$  is defined as

$$
\operatorname {I} _ {\text {I n f o L O O B}} \left(X _ {1}; Y\right) = \operatorname {E} _ {p (\boldsymbol {y})} \left[ \operatorname {E} _ {\tilde {p} (X | \boldsymbol {y})} \left[ \ln \left(\frac {f \left(\boldsymbol {x} _ {1} , \boldsymbol {y}\right)}{\frac {1}{N - 1} \sum_ {i = 2} ^ {N} f \left(\boldsymbol {x} _ {i} , \boldsymbol {y}\right)}\right) \right] \right]. \tag {4}
$$

For  $f(\pmb{x}, \pmb{y}) = p(\pmb{y} \mid \pmb{x})$  we obtain the InfoLOOB with probabilities.

Before we show that InfoLOOB is an upper bound on the mutual information, we have to define some expressions that are required for the proof.  $\tilde{p} (\pmb {x}\mid \pmb {y})$  draws the positives for  $\pmb{y}$  with lower probability than  $p(x)$ , that is, the positives are under-sampled.  $Z(\pmb {y}) = \operatorname{E}_{\tilde{p} (\pmb {x}|\pmb {y})}[f(\pmb {x},\pmb {y})]$  gives the average score  $f(\pmb {x},\pmb {y})$ , if the negatives for  $\pmb{y}$  are selected via  $\tilde{p} (\pmb {x}\mid \pmb {y})$ , in contrast to  $Z^{*}(\pmb {y}) = \operatorname{E}_{p(\pmb {x})}[f(\pmb {x},\pmb {y})]$ , which gives the average score  $f(\pmb {x},\pmb {y})$  if sampling from  $p(\pmb {x})$ . We define the variational distribution  $q(\pmb {x}\mid \pmb {y}) = \frac{p(\pmb{x})f(\pmb{x},\pmb{y})}{Z^{*}(\pmb{y})}$ . Our main assumption is expressed by the log-ratio of the averages  $Z(\pmb {y})$  and  $Z^{*}(\pmb {y})$ :

$$
\operatorname {E} _ {p (\boldsymbol {y})} \left[ \mathrm {K L} \left(p (\boldsymbol {x} \mid \boldsymbol {y}) \| q (\boldsymbol {x} \mid \boldsymbol {y})\right) \right] \leqslant \operatorname {E} _ {p (\boldsymbol {y})} \left[ \ln Z ^ {*} (\boldsymbol {y}) - \ln Z (\boldsymbol {y}) \right], \tag {5}
$$

which ensures that the positives  $\pmb{x}$  obtained via  $p(\pmb{x} \mid \pmb{y})$  are sufficiently under-sampled. The Kullback-Leibler divergence gives the minimal required gap between averaging  $f(\pmb{x}, \pmb{y})$  via  $p(\pmb{x})$  and averaging  $f(\pmb{x}, \pmb{y})$  via  $\tilde{p}(\pmb{x} \mid \pmb{y})$ .

The next theorem shows that InfoLOOB is an upper bound on the mutual information.

Theorem 2 (InfoLOOB upper bound). If  $\tilde{X} = \{\pmb{x}_2, \dots, \pmb{x}_N\}$  are drawn iid according to  $\tilde{p}(\pmb{x} \mid \pmb{y})$  and if the main assumption Eq. (5) holds, then InfoLOOB with score function  $f(\pmb{x}, \pmb{y})$  is an upper bound on the mutual information:

$$
\mathrm {I} \left(X _ {1}; Y\right) \leqslant \mathrm {E} _ {p (\boldsymbol {y})} \left[ \mathrm {E} _ {\tilde {p} (X | \boldsymbol {y})} \left[ \ln \left(\frac {f \left(\boldsymbol {x} _ {1} , \boldsymbol {y}\right)}{\frac {1}{N - 1} \sum_ {i = 2} ^ {N} f \left(\boldsymbol {x} _ {i} , \boldsymbol {y}\right)}\right) \right] \right] = \mathrm {I} _ {\text {I n f o L O O B}} \left(X _ {1}; Y\right). \tag {6}
$$

In particular, the bound holds if the negative samples  $\tilde{X} = \{\pmb{x}_2,\dots ,\pmb{x}_N\}$  are drawn iid according to  $p(\pmb {x})$  and  $f(\pmb {x},\pmb {y}) = p(\pmb {y}\mid \pmb {x})$ . Thus, the bound holds for InfoLOOB with probabilities without under-sampling.

The proof for this theorem is given as proof for Theorem A2 in the Appendix.

Gradient of the loss shows saturation of InfoNCE and the explaining away effect. For computing the loss function, we sample  $N$  pairs independently from  $p(\pmb{x},\pmb{y})$ , which gives the training set  $\{(\pmb{x}_1,\pmb{y}_1),(\pmb{x}_2,\pmb{y}_2),\dots,(\pmb{x}_N,\pmb{y}_N)\}$ . InfoNCE uses for the matrix of negative samples  $\pmb{X} = (x_{1},\ldots ,x_{N})$ , which contains the positive sample  $x_{1}$ . InfoLOOB is similar to InfoNCE except it uses  $\tilde{\pmb{X}} = (\pmb{x}_2,\dots,\pmb{x}_N)$  containing only negative samples.

The InfoNCE and the InfoLOOB loss are

$$
\mathrm {L} _ {\text {I n f o N C E}} = - \frac {1}{N} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {N} \ln \left(\frac {f \left(\boldsymbol {x} _ {i} , \boldsymbol {y} _ {i}\right)}{\frac {1}{N} \sum_ {j = 1} ^ {N} f \left(\boldsymbol {x} _ {j} , \boldsymbol {y} _ {i}\right)}\right) = \frac {1}{N} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {N} \mathrm {L} _ {\text {I n f o N C E}} (\boldsymbol {y} _ {i}), \tag {7}
$$

$$
\mathrm {L} _ {\text {I n f o L O O B}} = - \frac {1}{N} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {N} \ln \left(\frac {f \left(\boldsymbol {x} _ {i} , \boldsymbol {y} _ {i}\right)}{\frac {1}{N - 1} \sum_ {j = 1 , j \neq i} ^ {N} f \left(\boldsymbol {x} _ {j} , \boldsymbol {y} _ {i}\right)}\right) = \frac {1}{N} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {N} \mathrm {L} _ {\text {I n f o L O O B}} \left(\boldsymbol {y} _ {i}\right). \tag {8}
$$

For the score function  $f(\pmb{x}, \pmb{y})$ , we use  $f(\pmb{x}, \pmb{y}) = \exp(\tau^{-1} \sin(\pmb{x}, \pmb{y}))$  with the similarity  $\sin(\pmb{x}, \pmb{y}) = \pmb{y}^T \pmb{x}$  and  $\tau$  as the temperature. Therefore, the losses can be simplified to  $\mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{InfoNCE}}(\pmb{y}) = -\tau^{-1} \pmb{y}^T \pmb{x}_1 + \tau^{-1} \mathrm{lse}(\tau^{-1}, \pmb{X}^T \pmb{y})$  and  $\mathrm{L}_{\mathrm{InfoLOOB}}(\pmb{y}) = -\tau^{-1} \pmb{y}^T \pmb{x}_1 + \tau^{-1} \mathrm{lse}(\tau^{-1}, \tilde{\pmb{X}}^T \pmb{y})$ , where lse is the log-sum-exp function (see definition Eq. (A67) in the Appendix). The gradient of the InfoNCE loss with respect to  $\pmb{y}$  is  $-\tau^{-1} \pmb{x}_1 + \tau^{-1} \pmb{X}$  softmax  $(\tau^{-1} \pmb{X}^T \pmb{y})$  and the gradient of the InfoLOOB loss is  $-\tau^{-1} \pmb{x}_1 + \tau^{-1} \tilde{\pmb{X}}$  softmax  $(\tau^{-1} \tilde{\pmb{X}}^T \pmb{y})$ . Using  $p = (p_1, \dots, p_N)^T = \text{softmax}(\tau^{-1} \pmb{X}^T \pmb{y})$ , the gradient of InfoNCE with respect to  $\pmb{y}$  is  $-\tau^{-1}(1 - p_1)(\pmb{x}_1 - \tilde{\pmb{X}})$  and its gradient with respect to  $\pmb{x}_1$  is  $-\tau^{-1}(1 - p_1) \pmb{y}$  (see Appendix Subsection A.1.3). By and large, the gradient of InfoNCE is scaled by  $(1 - p_1)$  compared to the gradient of InfoLOOB, where  $p_1$  is softmax similarity between the anchor  $\pmb{y}$  and positive sample  $\pmb{x}_1$ . Consequently, for InfoNCE learning stalls when anchor and positive sample become similar to each other. The stalled learning is the reason for the explaining away effect of InfoNCE. One feature that is shared between anchor and positive sample can already lead to a high similarity while another shared feature is missed, that is, explained away.

# 3 CLOOB: INFOLOOB WITH MODERN HOPFIELD NETWORKS

We want to use InfoLOOB as objective, since it estimates the mutual information (MI) better and, in particular, works much better for large MI than InfoNCE. Cheng et al. (2020, Fig. 1 and Fig. 2) show that InfoLOOB is a better estimator for the MI than InfoNCE (van den Oord et al., 2018), MINE (Belghazi et al., 2018), and NWJ (Nguyen et al., 2010). We experimentally confirmed the superior quality of InfoLOOB over InfoNCE at estimating mutual information.

The reason for the low estimation quality of InfoNCE for large mutual information is the term in the ln of Eq. (2), which is smaller than  $N$  and bounds InfoNCE from above.

However, InfoLOOB has higher variance than lower bounds on MI like InfoNCE, which considerably hampers learning (Cheng et al., 2020, Fig. 1 and Fig. 2), see also Appendix Section A.2. The InfoNCE objective has the form  $a / (a + b)$  while InfoLOOB has the form  $a / b$  with  $a$  giving the anchor-to-positive similarity and  $b$  the average anchor-to-negative similarity. For small  $b$ , we observe high variance and instability of InfoLOOB stemming from a small denominator. Modern Hopfield networks (Ramsauer et al., 2021; 2020; Widrich et al., 2020) are a remedy for the high variance. Modern Hopfield networks substitute the original patterns by retrieved patterns, which are an average over the stored patterns. We tested the variance of MI estimators/bounds on toy tasks, with samples drawn from Gaussian distributions following (Belghazi et al., 2018; Poole et al., 2019; Cheng et al., 2020). With the InfoLOOB objective, we train deep learning architectures with and without modern Hopfield networks on top, where the current learning batch is stored in the modern Hopfield networks. We used training data with mutual information of 10 and 14, where the parameters were optimized for the best performance on a validation set. We test the final model on different levels of mutual information. Figure 1 shows that modern Hopfield networks reduce the variance of the model.

Our novel Contrastive Leave One Out Boost (CLOOB) uses the InfoLOOB objective together with modern Hopfield networks, where the original embeddings are substituted by retrieved embeddings. Modern Hopfield networks reduce the high variance of InfoLOOB, since the retrieved embeddings are less noisy and more similar to one another than the original embeddings. Modern Hopfield networks reinforce correlations in the data, since the retrieved embeddings have an enriched correlation structure through co-occurrences of embedding features.

Figure 2: Sketch of CLOOB for image-text pairs. The image embedding  $\boldsymbol{x}_i$  and the text embedding  $\boldsymbol{y}_i$  retrieve the embeddings  $U_{\boldsymbol{x}_i}$  and  $U_{\boldsymbol{y}_i}$ , respectively, from a modern Hopfield network that stores image embeddings  $U = (u_1, \ldots, u_M)$  (two green boxes in the left block). The retrieved image embedding  $U_{\boldsymbol{x}_i}$  serves as anchor in order to contrast the positive image embedding  $U_{\boldsymbol{y}_i}$  with the negative image embeddings  $U_{\boldsymbol{y}_j}$  for  $j \neq i$ . Analog, for the second modern Hopfield network that stores texts  $V = (v_1, \ldots, v_K)$  (two green boxes in the right block).

We have  $N$  pairs of embeddings  $\{(\pmb{x}_1,\pmb{y}_1),\dots,(\pmb{x}_N,\pmb{y}_N)\}$  that form the training set,  $M$  stored patterns  $\pmb{U} = (\pmb{u}_1,\dots,\pmb{u}_M)$  and  $K$  stored patterns  $\pmb{V} = (\pmb{v}_1,\dots,\pmb{v}_K)$ . The embeddings (query)  $\pmb{x}_i$  and  $\pmb{y}_i$  retrieve  $\pmb{U}_{\pmb{x}_i}$  and  $\pmb{U}_{\pmb{y}_i}$ , respectively, from  $\pmb{U}$  — analogous notation for retrievals from  $\pmb{V}$ . Both queries and stored patterns are normalized:  $\| \pmb{x}_i\| = \| \pmb{y}_i\| = \| \pmb{u}_i\| = \| \pmb{v}_i\| = 1$ . The following vectors are retrieved from modern Hopfield networks (Ramsauer et al., 2021; 2020; Widrich et al., 2020):

$$
\boldsymbol {U} _ {\boldsymbol {x} _ {i}} = \boldsymbol {U} \operatorname {s o f t m a x} \left(\beta \boldsymbol {U} ^ {T} \boldsymbol {x} _ {i}\right), \quad \boldsymbol {U} _ {\boldsymbol {y} _ {i}} = \boldsymbol {U} \operatorname {s o f t m a x} \left(\beta \boldsymbol {U} ^ {T} \boldsymbol {y} _ {i}\right), \tag {9}
$$

$$
\boldsymbol {V} _ {\boldsymbol {x} _ {i}} = \boldsymbol {V} \operatorname {s o f t m a x} \left(\beta \boldsymbol {V} ^ {T} \boldsymbol {x} _ {i}\right), \quad \boldsymbol {V} _ {\boldsymbol {y} _ {i}} = \boldsymbol {V} \operatorname {s o f t m a x} \left(\beta \boldsymbol {V} ^ {T} \boldsymbol {y} _ {i}\right). \tag {10}
$$

Here  $\beta$  is a hyperparameter corresponding to the inverse temperature:  $\beta = 0$  retrieves the average of the stored pattern, while large  $\beta$  retrieves the stored pattern that is most similar to the state pattern

(query). We have the InfoNCE and InfoLOOB loss functions:

$$
\mathrm {L} _ {\text {I n f o N C E}} = - \frac {1}{N} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {N} \ln \frac {\exp \left(\tau^ {- 1} \boldsymbol {x} _ {i} ^ {T} \boldsymbol {y} _ {i}\right)}{\sum_ {j = 1} ^ {N} \exp \left(\tau^ {- 1} \boldsymbol {x} _ {i} ^ {T} \boldsymbol {y} _ {j}\right)} - \frac {1}{N} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {N} \ln \frac {\exp \left(\tau^ {- 1} \boldsymbol {x} _ {i} ^ {T} \boldsymbol {y} _ {i}\right)}{\sum_ {j = 1} ^ {N} \exp \left(\tau^ {- 1} \boldsymbol {x} _ {j} ^ {T} \boldsymbol {y} _ {i}\right)}, \tag {11}
$$

$$
\mathrm {L} _ {\text {I n f o L O O B}} = - \frac {1}{N} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {N} \ln \frac {\exp \left(\tau^ {- 1} \boldsymbol {x} _ {i} ^ {T} \boldsymbol {y} _ {i}\right)}{\sum_ {j \neq i} ^ {N} \exp \left(\tau^ {- 1} \boldsymbol {x} _ {i} ^ {T} \boldsymbol {y} _ {j}\right)} - \frac {1}{N} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {N} \ln \frac {\exp \left(\tau^ {- 1} \boldsymbol {x} _ {i} ^ {T} \boldsymbol {y} _ {i}\right)}{\sum_ {j \neq i} ^ {N} \exp \left(\tau^ {- 1} \boldsymbol {x} _ {j} ^ {T} \boldsymbol {y} _ {i}\right)}. \tag {12}
$$

For CLOOB that uses the InfoLOOB loss, the embedded samples  $\boldsymbol{x}_i$  and  $\boldsymbol{y}_i$  are substituted by retrieved embedded samples. In the first term  $\boldsymbol{x}_i$  and  $\boldsymbol{y}_i$  are substituted by  $U_{\boldsymbol{x}_i}$  and  $U_{\boldsymbol{y}_i}$ , respectively, while in the second term by  $V_{\boldsymbol{x}_i}$  and  $V_{\boldsymbol{y}_i}$ . All retrieved samples are normalized,  $\| U_{\boldsymbol{x}_i} \| = \| U_{\boldsymbol{y}_i} \| = \| V_{\boldsymbol{x}_i} \| = \| V_{\boldsymbol{y}_i} \| = 1$ . We obtain the InfoLOOB loss function:

$$
\mathrm {L} _ {\text {I n f o L O O B}} = - \frac {1}{N} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {N} \ln \frac {\exp \left(\tau^ {- 1} \boldsymbol {U} _ {\boldsymbol {x} _ {i}} ^ {T} \boldsymbol {U} _ {\boldsymbol {y} _ {i}}\right)}{\sum_ {j \neq i} ^ {N} \exp \left(\tau^ {- 1} \boldsymbol {U} _ {\boldsymbol {x} _ {i}} ^ {T} \boldsymbol {U} _ {\boldsymbol {y} _ {j}}\right)} - \frac {1}{N} \sum_ {i = 1} ^ {N} \ln \frac {\exp \left(\tau^ {- 1} \boldsymbol {V} _ {\boldsymbol {x} _ {i}} ^ {T} \boldsymbol {V} _ {\boldsymbol {y} _ {i}}\right)}{\sum_ {j \neq i} ^ {N} \exp \left(\tau^ {- 1} \boldsymbol {V} _ {\boldsymbol {x} _ {j}} ^ {T} \boldsymbol {V} _ {\boldsymbol {y} _ {i}}\right)}. \tag {13}
$$

Fig. 2 sketches CLOOB with this loss function exemplified at image-text pairs. For the loss function Eq. (13), the dot product between the anchor retrieval and the positive pattern retrieval has low variance and reinforces the covariance structure in the data as elaborated in the following.

High variance of  $U_{x_i}^T V_{y_i}$ . We did not use a loss function that contains dot products like  $U_{x_i}^T V_{y_i}$ , because these dot products have higher variance than the ones we have used. Beyond  $x_i$  and  $y_i$ , the dot product  $U_{x_i}^T V_{y_i}$  requires  $M + K$  stored patterns, while  $U_{x_i}^T U_{y_i}$  and  $V_{x_i}^T V_{y_i}$  require  $M$  and  $K$ , respectively. Therefore,  $U_{x_i}^T V_{y_i}$  is assumed to have higher variance.

Covariance structure extracted by  $U_{\boldsymbol{x}_i}^T U_{\boldsymbol{y}_i}$  and  $V_{\boldsymbol{x}_i}^T V_{\boldsymbol{y}_i}$ . The Jacobian  $J$  of the softmax  $\boldsymbol{p} =$  softmax  $(\beta \boldsymbol{a})$  is  $J(\beta \boldsymbol{a}) = \beta (\mathrm{diag}(\boldsymbol{p}) - \boldsymbol{p}\boldsymbol{p}^T)$ . We define the weighted covariance  $\operatorname{Cov}(U)$ , where sample  $\boldsymbol{u}_i$  is drawn with probability  $p_i$ , as  $[\operatorname{Cov}(U)]_{kl} = [UJ(\beta \boldsymbol{a})U^T]_{kl} = \beta (\sum_{i=1}^{M} p_i u_{ik} u_{il} - \sum_{i=1}^{M} p_i u_{ik} \sum_{i=1}^{M} p_i u_{il})$ . The formula of the weighted covariance differs from the standard empirical covariance since the factor  $1/M$  is replaced by  $p_i$ . Thus  $\boldsymbol{u}_i$  is sampled with probability  $p_i$  instead of being sampled uniformly with probability  $1/M$ .

We apply the mean value theorem to the softmax function with mean Jacobian matrix  $\mathrm{J}^{\mathrm{m}}(\beta \pmb{a}) = \int_0^1\mathrm{J}(\lambda \beta \pmb {a})\mathrm{d}\lambda$ . The mean Jacobian  $\mathrm{J}^{\mathrm{m}}(\beta \pmb {a})$  is a symmetric, diagonally dominant, positive semi-definite matrix with one eigenvalue of zero for eigenvector 1 and spectral norm bounded by  $\| \mathbf{J}^{\mathrm{m}}\| _2\leqslant 0.5\beta$  (see Appendix Lemma A1). We can express  $U_{x_i}^T U_{y_i}$  as (see Appendix Theorem A3):

$$
\boldsymbol {U} _ {\boldsymbol {x} _ {i}} ^ {T} \boldsymbol {U} _ {\boldsymbol {y} _ {i}} = (\bar {\boldsymbol {u}} + \operatorname {C o v} (\boldsymbol {U}, \boldsymbol {x} _ {i}) \boldsymbol {x} _ {i}) ^ {T} (\bar {\boldsymbol {u}} + \operatorname {C o v} (\boldsymbol {U}, \boldsymbol {y} _ {i}) \boldsymbol {y} _ {i}), \tag {14}
$$

where the mean is  $\bar{\pmb{u}} = 1 / M\pmb{U}\pmb{1}$  and the weighted covariances are  $\mathrm{Cov}(\pmb {U},\pmb {x}_i) = \pmb {U}\mathrm{J}^{\mathrm{m}}(\beta \pmb {U}^{T}\pmb {x}_{i})\pmb{U}^{T}$  and  $\mathrm{Cov}(\pmb {U},\pmb {y}_i) = \pmb {U}\mathrm{J}^{\mathrm{m}}(\beta \pmb {U}^{T}\pmb {y}_i)\pmb{U}^{T}$ . The weighted covariance  $\mathrm{Cov}(\pmb {U},.)$  is the covariance if the stored pattern  $\pmb{u}_i$  is drawn according to an averaged  $p_i$  given by  $\mathrm{J}^{\mathrm{m}}(.)$ . When maximizing the dot product  $\pmb{U}_{\pmb{x}_i}^T\pmb{U}_{\pmb{y}_i}$ , the normalized vectors  $\pmb{x}_i$  and  $\pmb{y}_i$  are encouraged to agree on drawing the patterns  $\pmb{u}_i$  with the same probability  $p_i$  in order to generate similar weighted covariance matrices  $\mathrm{Cov}(\pmb {U},.)$ . If subsets of  $\pmb{U}$  have a strong covariance structure, then it can be exploited to produce large weighted covariances and, in turn, large dot products of  $\pmb{U}_{\pmb{x}_i}^T\pmb {U}_{\pmb{y}_i}$ . Furthermore, for a large dot product  $\pmb{U}_{\pmb{x}_i}^T\pmb {U}_{\pmb{y}_i}$ ,  $\pmb{x}_i$  and  $\pmb{y}_i$  have to be similar to each other to extract the same direction from the covariance matrices. Above considerations for  $\pmb{U}_{\pmb{x}_i}^T\pmb {U}_{\pmb{y}_i}$  analogously apply to  $\pmb{V}_{\pmb{x}_i}^T\pmb{V}_{\pmb{y}_i}$ .

Training samples reused as stored patterns. To be data efficient in our experiments, we use the training samples also as the patterns that are stored in the modern Hopfield network. Hence, we set  $\boldsymbol{u}_i = \boldsymbol{x}_i$  and  $\boldsymbol{v}_i = \boldsymbol{y}_i$ , that is,  $U = X$  and  $V = Y$ . Consequently, we store the learning batch in the modern Hopfield networks as  $U$  and  $V$ . In particular this means that  $x_i$  can retrieve itself from  $U = X$  but not from  $V = Y$ . Analogously,  $y_i$  can retrieve itself from  $V = Y$  but not from  $U = X$ .

Model embeddings  $x$  and  $y$  vs. retrieved embeddings  $U_x, U_y, V_x,$  and  $V_y$ . After learning, both the model embeddings  $x$  and  $y$  as well as the retrieved embeddings  $U_x, U_y, V_x,$  and  $V_y$  may serve for the downstream tasks, e.g. for zero-shot transfer learning. When using the retrieved embeddings,

the modern Hopfield networks have to be filled with stored embedded patterns, which can be random samples, prototypes, templates, or proprietary samples. In this case the final retrieval depends on the embeddings that are stored in the modern Hopfield network.

# 4 EXPERIMENTS

We compare our new approach CLOOB to CLIP (Radford et al., 2021a;b) for their capability of zero-shot transfer learning on two pretraining datasets. The first dataset, Conceptual Captions (CC) (Sharma et al., 2018), has a very rich textual description of images but only three million image-text pairs. The second dataset, a subset of YFCC100M (Thomee et al., 2016), has 15 million image-text pairs but the textual description is less rich than for CC and often vacuous. For both pretraining datasets the downstream zero-shot transfer learning performance is tested on seven image classification datasets.

# 4.1 CONCEPTUAL CAPTIONS PRETRAINING

Pretraining dataset. The Conceptual Captions (CC) (Sharma et al., 2018) dataset consists of 2.9 million images and corresponding high-quality captions. Images and their corresponding notations of CC have been gathered via an automated process from the web and therefore represent a wide variety of styles. Raw descriptions of images are collected from the alt-text HTML attribute. Both images and texts are filtered such that only image-text pairs above a certain quality threshold are part of this dataset.

Methods compared. We compare our new approach CLOOB to CLIP (Radford et al., 2021a;b). The CLOOB implementation is based on OpenCLIP (Ilharco et al., 2021), which achieves results equivalent to CLIP on the YFCC dataset (see Section 4.2). OpenCLIP also reports results on the CC dataset. As CLIP does not train models on CC we report results from this reimplementation as baseline. Analogously to CLIP (Radford et al., 2021a, Section 2.4), we use the modified ResNet (He et al., 2016) and BERT (Devlin et al., 2018; 2019) architectures to encode image and text input. As ResNet encoders we consider ResNet-50, ResNet-101 and ResNet-50x4.

Hyperparameter selection and learning schedule. We use the hyperparameters of OpenCLIP, concretely, a learning rate of  $1 \times 10^{-3}$  and a weight decay of 0.1 for the Adam optimizer (Kingma et al., 2014) with decoupled weight decay regularization (Loshchilov & Hutter, 2019). Different from OpenCLIP we use a batch size of 512 due to computational restraints. This change did not result in performance loss. The learning rate scheduler for all experiments is cosine annealing with warmup and hard restarts (Loshchilov & Hutter, 2017). We report the hyperparameter  $\tau$  (default 0.07) from CLIP as  $\tau^{-1}$  of 14.3 to be in the same regime as the hyperparameter  $\beta$  for the modern Hopfield networks. The main hyperparameter search for CLOOB (also for YFCC pretraining in the next section) was done with ResNet-50 as the vision encoder. Since a learnable  $\tau^{-1}$  in combination with the InfoLOOB loss results in undesired learning behavior (see Appendix Section A.1.3) we set  $\tau^{-1}$  to a fixed value of 30, which was determined via hyperparameter search (see Appendix Section A.3.2). For the modern Hopfield networks, the hyperparameter  $\beta$  was set to 8. Further we scale the loss in Eq. (13) with  $\tau$  to remove the factor  $\tau^{-1}$  from the gradients (see Appendix Section A.1.3) resulting in the loss function  $\tau L_{InfoLOOB}$ .

Evaluation metrics: Zero-shot transfer learning. We evaluate and compare both CLIP and CLOOB on their zero-shot transfer learning capabilities on the following downstream image classification tasks. Birdsnap (Berg et al., 2014) contains images of 500 different North American bird species. The Country211 (Radford et al., 2021a;b) dataset consists of photos across 211 countries and is designed to test the geolocation capability of visual representations. Flowers102 (Nilsback & Zisserman, 2008) is a dataset containing images of 102 flower species. GTSRB (Stallkamp et al., 2011) contains images for classification of German traffic signs. UCF101 (Soomro et al., 2012) is a video dataset with short clips for action recognition. For UCF101 we follow the procedure reported in CLIP and extract the middle frame of every video to assemble the dataset. Stanford Cars (Krause et al., 2013) contains images of 196 types of cars. ImageNet (Deng et al., 2009) is a large scale image classification dataset with images across 1,000 classes. ImageNetv2 (Recht et al., 2019a;b) consists of three new test sets with 10,000 images each for the ImageNet benchmark. For further details see Appendix Section A.3.3.

Ablation studies. CLOOB has two new major components compared to CLIP: (1) the InfoLOOB objective instead of the InfoNCE objective and (2) the modern Hopfield networks. To assess which of the new major components of CLOOB has led to the performance increase over CLIP, we performed ablation studies on the CC dataset. First, we enhanced CLIP by replacing the InfoNCE objective with InfoLOOB. In general, the InfoLOOB objective increases the performance of CLIP but not for all datasets (see Appendix Section A.3.1). Next, we added modern Hopfield networks to the CLIP architecture and used retrieved embeddings instead of the original embeddings, while keeping the InfoNCE objective. The performance clearly dropped compared to the original CLIP (see Appendix Section A.3.1). We attribute the performance drop to the saturation of InfoNCE, which is reinforced by the smoothing of modern Hopfield networks. CLOOB has both new components: it adds modern Hopfield networks to CLIP and replaces the InfoNCE objective with InfoLOOB. CLOOB dramatically improves the performance on 7 out of 8 zero-shot transfer learning tasks compared to CLIP. An additional ablation study considers the influence of the learning rate scheduler. The results of the ablation studies are reported in Appendix Section A.3.1.

# 4.2 YFCC PRETRAINING

Pretraining dataset. To establish a comparison with CLIP, we use the same subset of 15 million samples from the YFCC100M dataset (Thomee et al., 2016), which we refer to as YFCC. This subset was created by filtering YFCC100M for images which contain natural language descriptions and/or titles in English. It was not filtered by quality of the captions, therefore the textual descriptions are less rich and contain superfluous information. The dataset with 400 million samples used to train the models in CLIP has not been released and, thus, is not available for comparison. Due to limited computational resources we are unable to compare our method to CLIP on other datasets of this size.

Methods compared and evaluation. In addition to the comparison of CLIP and CLOOB based on the OpenCLIP reimplementation as in the previous subsection, we include the original CLIP results as reported by OpenAI (Radford et al., 2021a, Table 12) as a baseline.

Hyperparameter selection. We reuse the hyperparameters we selected on the Conceptual Captions dataset except learning rate, batch size and  $\beta$ . For the modern Hopfield network the hyperparameter  $\beta$  is set to 14.3 which is the default CLIP parameter for  $\tau^{-1}$  in the InfoNCE objective. Furthermore, the learning rate is set to  $5 \times 10^{-4}$  and a batch size of 1024 as in OpenCLIP is selected. For further details see Appendix Section A.3.2.

Evaluation metrics. Evaluation metrics are again zero-shot transfer learning capabilities on downstream tasks as in the previous experiment.

# 5 CONCLUSION

We have introduced "Contrastive Leave One Out Boost" (CLOOB), a method in which modern Hopfield networks boost learning with the InfoLOOB objective. We have demonstrated that modern Hopfield networks increase stability and reinforce correlations for contrastive learning. Theoretical properties of the InfoLOOB bound and the InfoLOOB objective are shown and opposed to InfoNCE. The results of our experiments suggest InfoLOOB as an alternative to InfoNCE in contrastive learning approaches. An ablation study shows that both components, the InfoLOOB objective and modern Hopfield networks, are necessary to yield high performance. At a set of seven downstream tasks, the novel CLOOB method and CLIP are compared after pretraining on Conceptual Captions and the YFCC dataset with respect to their zero-shot transfer learning performance. CLOOB consistently outperforms CLIP at zero-shot transfer learning across all considered architectures and datasets.

# ETHICAL CONSIDERATIONS

Impact on ML and related scientific fields. Our research has the potential to positively impact a wide variety of fields of life due to its general applicability. Most importantly, it has the potential to reduce the cost for training other AI systems, which could lead to a reduction of compute costs and carbon dioxide emissions.

However, any new development in machine learning can be applied for good or for bad. Our system can be used for medical applications where it could save lives but might also be used for surveillance and malevolent systems.

Impact on society. A potential danger could arise from an application of our approach in which users rely overly on the outcomes. For example, in a medical setting, physicians might rely on the technical system and shift the liability towards the machine. This might also happen in the domain of self-driving cars, when drivers start paying less attention to the traffic because of an AI-based driving system. Finally, our method may also be deployed in companies to automate various simple tasks, which might lead to a reduced need for particular jobs in production systems.

Consequences of failures of the method. Depending on the application area, a failure of this method might be of lesser concern, such as a failed execution of a computer program. If our method is employed within a larger automation system, a failure could result in damages such as a car accident or errors of a production system. However, this holds for almost all machine learning methods, and their usage and testing depends on the application area.

Leveraging of biases in the data and potential discrimination. Our proposed method relies on human-annotated data and thereby human decisions, which are usually strongly biased. The undesirable biases contained in dataset are learned and may propagate to downstream applications. Therefore, the responsible use of our method depends on a careful selection of the training data and awareness of the potential biases within those.
